content.overview: Section 531 BNSS governs the repeal of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 and enacts the critical transitional savings architecture. Under Section 531(2)(a), any appeal, application, trial, inquiry, or investigation pending immediately before 1 July 2024 must be continued and disposed of strictly in accordance with the 1973 CrPC as if the BNSS had not come into force, safeguarding vested rights and delineating the procedural boundary with Article 20(1) of the Constitution.
content.glance: Section 531 BNSS governs the repeal of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 and enacts the critical transitional savings architecture. Under Section 531(2)(a), any appeal, application, trial, inquiry, or investigation pending immediately before 1 July 2024 must be continued and disposed of strictly in accordance with the 1973 CrPC as if the BNSS had not come into force, safeguarding vested rights and delineating the procedural boundary with Article 20(1) of the Constitution.
content.study:
I. STATUTORY ARCHITECTURE & TRANSITIONAL JURISPRUDENCE
The repeal of a foundational procedural code that governed the Republic for fifty years (CrPC 1973) and its replacement by the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) on 1 July 2024 necessitated a comprehensive savings clause. Section 531 BNSS fulfills this constitutional and administrative necessity, mirroring yet refining the historical transition seen in Section 484 of the 1973 Code.

Section 531 operates as the jurisdictional fulcrum deciding whether police officers, magistrates, sessions judges, and high courts must apply the pre-existing 1973 Code or the newly enacted 2023 Sanhita. Misapplication of this transitional boundary creates fatal jurisdictional defects, rendering orders null and void ab initio.

II. TEXTUAL DECONSTRUCTION OF SECTION 531(2)(a)
Section 531(2)(a) provides:
"if, immediately before the date on which this Sanhita comes into force, there is any appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation pending, then, such appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation shall be disposed of, continued, held or made, as the case may be, in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, as in force immediately before such date, as if this Sanhita had not come into force."

The operative words "pending immediately before the date on which this Sanhita comes into force" establish a strict temporal and procedural threshold. Five distinct categories of legal proceedings are saved:
1. Pending Investigations: Where an FIR was registered on or before 30 June 2024, the investigation was "pending" on the eve of commencement. Consequently, the entire investigation, police report / chargesheet under s. 173 CrPC (not s. 193 BNSS), committal under s. 209 CrPC (not s. 232 BNSS), and subsequent trial continue under the 1973 Code.
2. Pending Inquiries & Trials: Any inquiry (e.g. s. 202 CrPC) or trial in which charges were framed or proceedings were active on or before 30 June 2024 must be held and concluded under CrPC 1973.
3. Pending Applications: Bail applications, revisions, Section 482 quashing petitions, and interlocutory motions filed prior to 1 July 2024 remain governed by the CrPC.
4. Pending Appeals: Criminal appeals instituted on or before 30 June 2024 are heard and disposed of under Chapter XXIX of the CrPC.

III. THE THREE PROCEDURAL EPOCHS IN INDIAN CRIMINAL PRACTICE
To determine the applicable law, the criminal bar must categorize every brief into one of three distinct epochs:
1. Epoch 1 — Incident & FIR Prior to 1 July 2024:
   - Substantive Law: Indian Penal Code, 1860.
   - Procedural Law: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (saved by Section 531(2)(a)).
   - Evidentiary Law: Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (saved by Section 170(2)(a) BSA).
2. Epoch 2 — Incident Prior to 1 July 2024, but FIR Registered on or after 1 July 2024:
   - Substantive Law: Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Article 20(1) constitutional bar prevents retrospective penal enhancement or new BNS offences).
   - Procedural Law: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (because NO investigation was pending immediately before 1 July 2024; procedural amendments apply prospectively from commencement).
   - Evidentiary Law: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (Section 63 certificate regime applies to evidence tendered post-1 July 2024).
3. Epoch 3 — Incident & FIR on or after 1 July 2024:
   - Substantive Law: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
   - Procedural Law: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.
   - Evidentiary Law: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.

IV. CONSTITUTIONAL INTERACTION WITH ARTICLE 20(1)
Article 20(1) of the Constitution guarantees two distinct protections:
1. Protection against ex post facto penalization: No person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged.
2. Protection against enhanced penalty: No person shall be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence.

Crucially, Article 20(1) protects substantive penal liability; it does NOT confer a vested right in any particular course of procedure (Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh v. State of V.P. (1953) SCR 1188; Union of India v. Sukumar Pyne (1966) 2 SCR 34). Therefore, while the substantive definition and penalty must strictly remain IPC for pre-July 2024 acts, Parliament possessed full constitutional competence to apply BNSS procedure to new investigations initiated post-1 July 2024.

V. EMERGENCE OF HIGH COURT JURISPRUDENCE ON APPEALS & BAIL
In Abdul Khader v. State of Kerala (2024) and Deepak Kumar v. State (Delhi HC, 2024), High Courts addressed whether an appeal filed AFTER 1 July 2024 against a conviction rendered in a CrPC trial should be filed under CrPC Section 374 or BNSS Section 528:
- The right of appeal is not a mere matter of procedure; it is a substantive statutory right that vests in the litigant at the commencement of the lis (Garikapati Veeraya v. N. Subbiah Choudhry, AIR 1957 SC 540).
- Where the trial was pending immediately before 1 July 2024, Section 531(2)(a) saves the entire cascade of statutory remedies under the CrPC. However, procedural filing mechanics (numbering, presentation) in the High Court registry are governed by the currently applicable rules of court.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective & Codification of Transitional Savings
sections.body:
The enactment of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) on 1 July 2024 formally repealed the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Act No. 2 of 1974) pursuant to Section 531(1).
In any comprehensive procedural reform, sudden discontinuity in ongoing investigations and trials across thousands of subordinate courts would paralyze the criminal justice system and violate due process under Article 21.
Section 531(2) was enacted to ensure institutional continuity by enacting a comprehensive savings clause, preserving ongoing investigations, inquiries, trials, applications, and appeals.
The doctrinal objective is the protection of legitimate procedural expectations and the avoidance of procedural chaos by enacting the legal fiction that the 1973 Code continues in force for all matters pending on 30 June 2024.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy & Deconstruction of Sub-sections (1) and (2)
sections.body:
Section 531(1) explicitly repeals the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, terminating its operation as the primary procedural code of India from 1 July 2024.
Section 531(2)(a) is the core savings clause. It contains four operative components: (a) temporal marker: "immediately before the date on which this Sanhita comes into force"; (b) subject-matter scope: "any appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation pending"; (c) governing law: "shall be disposed of, continued, held or made... in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973"; and (d) statutory fiction: "as if this Sanhita had not come into force".
Section 531(2)(b) preserves notifications, orders, appointments, powers, rules, forms, and licenses issued under the 1973 Code, continuing their legal validity insofar as they are not inconsistent with the provisions of BNSS.
Section 531(2)(c) governs statutory concordance, ensuring that references in other central or state statutes to the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 shall be construed as references to the BNSS.

sections.heading: The Mandatory Gateway: "Pending Immediately Before 1 July 2024"
sections.body:
Condition 1 — Temporal Test: The proceeding must have had legal existence at 23:59:59 on 30 June 2024. If an investigation was ongoing under a registered FIR, Section 531(2)(a) attaches to the entire continuum of that case.
Condition 2 — Continuum of Investigation to Trial: When an investigation is saved under s. 531(2)(a), the subsequent police report (s. 173 CrPC), cognizance (s. 190 CrPC), process (s. 204 CrPC), committal (s. 209 CrPC), and trial before the Sessions Court or Magistrate remain governed by the 1973 CrPC.
Condition 3 — The Unregistered FIR Boundary: Where an alleged criminal act occurred in 2023, but the victim registers an FIR only on 15 July 2024, no investigation was pending immediately before 1 July 2024. The investigation must be conducted under BNSS, while the substantive charge remains IPC.
Condition 4 — Interlocutory Applications: Bail applications under Section 437/439 CrPC filed after 1 July 2024 in a pre-July 2024 FIR: The Punjab & Haryana High Court and Delhi High Court have clarified that because the investigation itself is saved under s. 531(2)(a), bail remedies continue to flow from the CrPC framework.

sections.heading: Evidentiary Burdens under BSA 2023 (ss. 104–106 & s. 170)
sections.body:
Evidentiary Savings under Section 170 BSA: The counterpart to Section 531 BNSS is Section 170 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023. Section 170(2)(a) provides that any proceeding pending immediately before 1 July 2024 shall be governed by the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
Burden of Establishing Gateway: Under Section 104 BSA, any party asserting that a proceeding is governed by the CrPC 1973 carries the threshold burden of producing the certified copy of the FIR, complaint, or order showing that the matter was pending prior to 1 July 2024.
Electronic Evidence in Pre-July Trials: If a trial is saved under Section 531(2)(a) BNSS and Section 170(2)(a) BSA, digital evidence is tendered under Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (following Arjun Khotkar), not under Section 63 BSA.
Evidence Tendered in Post-July Investigations: If the FIR was registered post-1 July 2024 for a pre-July offence, the investigation follows BNSS and evidence must strictly adhere to Section 63 BSA and the statutory Schedule.

sections.heading: Procedural Roadmap, Forum & Common Preliminary Objections
sections.body:
Preliminary Objection on Misnumbered Petitions: A common preliminary objection raised by registry or public prosecutors is the filing of petitions under the CrPC after 1 July 2024. The advocate must demonstrate that the FIR or original trial was pending on 30 June 2024, attracting the protection of Section 531(2)(a).
Vested Right of Appeal: In Garikapati Veeraya (1957), the Supreme Court established that the right of appeal vests at the date of the initiation of the lis. An accused convicted in 2025 in a trial pending on 30 June 2024 retains the right of appeal under Section 374 CrPC.
Police Remand Jurisdictional Clash: Under Section 167 CrPC, police custody remand was restricted to the first 15 days. Under Section 187 BNSS, police custody can be sought in parts across 40 or 60 days. In an investigation pending on 30 June 2024, the police CANNOT invoke the expanded 40/60 day remand under BNSS s. 187; they are strictly bound by the 15-day ceiling of s. 167 CrPC pursuant to Section 531(2)(a).
Judicial Rectification: If an investigating agency erroneously files a chargesheet under Section 193 BNSS for a pre-July 2024 FIR, the Sessions Court / Magistrate has the inherent power to treat it as a police report under Section 173 CrPC under the doctrine of substance over form.

examples.title: Illustration 1 — Pending Investigation Governed by CrPC (Section 531(2)(a) Applies)
examples.body: An FIR was registered at Police Station Connaught Place on 15 June 2024 under Sections 420 and 406 IPC for criminal breach of trust. On 10 August 2024 (post-commencement of BNSS), the investigating officer files a chargesheet and seeks 15 days of police custody of the accused who was arrested on 8 August 2024, after having already spent 10 days in judicial custody. The IO invokes BNSS Section 187, arguing police custody can be granted in parts during the first 40 days. The defense counsel objects under BNSS Section 531(2)(a). The Magistrate rightly holds that because the investigation was pending immediately before 1 July 2024, the entire investigation remains governed by the 1973 CrPC. Under Section 167(2) CrPC, police custody is permissible only during the initial 15 days from arrest. The prayer for police custody is rejected.

examples.title: Illustration 2 — New FIR for Pre-July Offence (BNSS Procedure Applies)
examples.body: A burglary takes place at a commercial warehouse in December 2023. However, the owner was overseas and discovers the loss only in September 2024. The FIR is registered on 20 September 2024. The defense argues that since the burglary occurred prior to 1 July 2024, the police must follow the 1973 CrPC and cannot use BNSS procedures such as audio-video recording of search and seizure under BNSS Section 105. The objection fails. Because NO investigation, inquiry, or trial was pending immediately before 1 July 2024, Section 531(2)(a) has no application. While the substantive offence is charged under Section 380/457 IPC pursuant to Article 20(1), the entire investigation and trial procedure must strictly follow the BNSS 2023.

hypotheticals.question: As Senior Counsel appearing for Ananya, evaluate the legality of the police remand application and determine the governing procedural code under Section 531(2)(a) BNSS.
hypotheticals.analysis:
1. Inviolability of Section 531(2)(a): FIR No. 120/2024 was registered on 25 May 2024. As of 23:59:59 on 30 June 2024, the investigation had legal existence and was pending. Section 531(2)(a) mandates that such an investigation "shall be disposed of, continued, held or made... in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973... as if this Sanhita had not come into force."
2. Rejection of BNSS Police Custody: Because CrPC 1973 governs the investigation, Section 167(2) CrPC applies. Under the settled law of Central Bureau of Investigation v. Anupam J. Kulkarni (1992) 3 SCC 141, police custody cannot be granted beyond the first 15 days from the date of initial remand. Since Ananya was remanded on 20 July 2024, the 15-day window expired in early August 2024. The police cannot invoke Section 187 BNSS to obtain split custody in September 2024. The application is legally incompetent.
3. Form of the Chargesheet: The captioning of the chargesheet under Section 193 BNSS is technically erroneous, as it must be submitted under Section 173 CrPC. However, under the doctrine of nomenclature not overriding substance, the court will treat the document as a police report under Section 173 CrPC and take cognizance under Section 190(1)(b) CrPC.
4. Procedural Order: The Special Judge must dismiss the police remand application with prejudice and direct the registry to register the case as a Sessions Case under the CrPC 1973.

distinctions.title: Investigation Pending on 30 June 2024 vs Investigation Commenced on or after 1 July 2024

rows.left: Section 531(2)(a) BNSS: saved as if BNSS had not come into force.
rows.right: Section 1(2) & 531(1) BNSS: governed prospectively by the BNSS.

rows.left: Section 167(2) CrPC: restricted strictly to the first 15 days from arrest.
rows.right: Section 187(3) BNSS: police remand permissible in parts during first 40 or 60 days.

rows.left: Optional under CrPC guidelines, not mandatory under the statutory code.
rows.right: Strictly mandatory under Section 105 BNSS (mandatory videography of seizure).

rows.left: Governed by Section 41, 41A, 41B CrPC and Arnesh Kumar guidelines.
rows.right: Governed by Section 35 BNSS, requiring designated police officer approval for senior citizens / minor offences.

distinctions.title: Substantive Ex Post Facto Protection (Art. 20(1)) vs Procedural Change (BNSS s. 531)

rows.left: Protected by Fundamental Right under Article 20(1) against retrospective penalization.
rows.right: No vested fundamental right in any specific procedure or forum (Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh).

rows.left: Strictly prospective: an act committed on 28 June 2024 CANNOT be punished under BNS 2023.
rows.right: Applies to new investigations of past acts unless saved by Section 531(2)(a).

rows.left: The accused cannot be subjected to a penalty greater than that permissible under the old law.
rows.right: Procedural modifications (e.g. video conferencing, summons via electronic means) apply immediately.

misconceptions.trap: If an offence was committed before 1 July 2024, the investigation must always be conducted under the 1973 CrPC.
misconceptions.correction: False. Section 531(2)(a) saves the CrPC procedure ONLY if the investigation was "pending immediately before" 1 July 2024. If the crime occurred in 2023 but the FIR is registered on or after 1 July 2024, no investigation was pending on the cut-off date. Therefore, the investigation must be conducted under BNSS 2023, while the substantive charge remains under the IPC pursuant to Article 20(1).

misconceptions.trap: An appeal filed after 1 July 2024 against a conviction rendered in a CrPC trial is completely governed by BNSS.
misconceptions.correction: False. In Garikapati Veeraya (1957) and reiterated by High Courts in 2024, the right of appeal is a substantive vested right created at the institution of the original proceedings. Under Section 531(2)(a), because the trial was pending immediately before 1 July 2024, the substantive right of appeal is saved under Section 374 CrPC.

misconceptions.trap: Police can seek split remand under Section 187 BNSS in old pending FIRs because remand is an ongoing procedural step.
misconceptions.correction: False. Section 531(2)(a) mandates that the pending investigation must be made "as if this Sanhita had not come into force". The investigating agency cannot cherry-pick advantageous BNSS provisions like split custody while investigating a pre-July 2024 FIR; they are bound by Section 167 CrPC.

cases.name: Garikapati Veeraya v. N. Subbiah Choudhry
cases.bench: Constitution Bench (S.R. Das, C.J., Venkatarama Ayyar, B.P. Sinha, S.K. Das, P. Govinda Menon, JJ.)
cases.facts: A suit was instituted prior to the commencement of the Constitution of India. An appeal arose after the Constitution came into force, raising the question of whether the right of appeal was governed by the pre-existing law or the new constitutional appellate provisions.
cases.issue: Whether the right of appeal is a vested right that arises at the date of the initiation of proceedings, and whether a new procedural enactment extinguishes that vested right.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The right of appeal is not a mere matter of procedure but is a substantive right. The institution of the suit or criminal proceeding carries with it the implication that all rights of appeal then in force are preserved to the parties until the rest of the career of the suit. This vested right can be taken away only by a subsequent enactment if it so provides expressly or by necessary intendment, and not otherwise.
cases.holding: Held that the right of appeal is governed by the law in force at the time of the institution of the proceeding.
cases.relevance: The foundational authority establishing that appeals arising from trials pending on 30 June 2024 remain substantively governed by the 1973 CrPC under Section 531(2)(a).

cases.name: State of Punjab v. Mohar Singh
cases.bench: Constitution Bench (M.C. Mahajan, C.J., B.K. Mukherjea, Vivian Bose, B. Jagannadhadas, T.L. Venkatarama Ayyar, JJ.)
cases.facts: The East Punjab Refugees (Registration of Land Claims) Act, 1948 repealed a 1947 Ordinance without an express savings clause in the new enactment. The respondent was prosecuted after the repeal for an offence committed during the currency of the Ordinance.
cases.issue: How a repeal without an express savings clause operates, and the scope of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 in preserving liabilities and investigations.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Whenever there is a repeal of an enactment, the consequences laid down in Section 6 of the General Clauses Act follow unless, as the section itself says, a different intention appears. The court must look to the provisions of the new Act to see whether they indicate a different intention and whether the previous rights and liabilities are preserved.
cases.holding: Held that prosecution for acts committed under the repealed Ordinance was preserved by Section 6 of the General Clauses Act.
cases.relevance: Leading authority on the interpretation of statutory repeal and savings provisions, controlling the operation of Section 531 BNSS.

cases.name: Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh v. State of Vindhya Pradesh
cases.bench: Constitution Bench (M. Patanjali Sastri, C.J., B.K. Mukherjea, Vivian Bose, Ghulam Hasan, B. Jagannadhadas, JJ.)
cases.facts: The appellants were prosecuted for offences under the Vindhya Pradesh Ordinance committed prior to the commencement of the Constitution of India, and challenged the procedure of trial as violating Article 20(1).
cases.issue: Whether Article 20(1) of the Constitution prohibits changes in criminal procedure or the forum of trial for offences committed prior to the amendment.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Article 20(1) prohibits convictions and penalties under ex post facto laws; it does NOT prohibit changes in procedure or the forum of trial. A person accused of an offence has no vested right in a particular course of procedure or in being tried by a specific court, provided the procedure applied does not amount to an ex post facto enhancement of penalty or deprivation of fair trial.
cases.holding: Upheld the application of new procedural rules to the trial of offences committed prior to the procedural amendment.
cases.relevance: The authoritative constitutional benchmark establishing that BNSS procedure can lawfully govern new investigations of pre-July 2024 offences without infringing Article 20(1).

cases.name: Abdul Khader v. State of Kerala
cases.facts: The petitioner was convicted by the Sessions Court in a trial held under the CrPC 1973. The judgment of conviction was pronounced on 28 June 2024. The petitioner filed an appeal before the High Court on 5 July 2024, styling it under Section 374 CrPC. The registry objected that the appeal must be filed under Section 528 BNSS.
cases.issue: Whether an appeal filed on or after 1 July 2024 challenging a conviction passed in a trial conducted under the 1973 CrPC should be filed under Section 374 CrPC or Section 528 BNSS.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Applying Section 531(2)(a) BNSS and Garikapati Veeraya, the trial was pending immediately before 1 July 2024, and the right of appeal had already crystallized. The appeal is substantively governed by Section 374 CrPC. The registry was directed to number and entertain the appeal under the CrPC.
cases.holding: Appeals arising from trials that were pending or concluded prior to 1 July 2024 are maintainable and saved under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
cases.relevance: Contemporary post-2024 judicial precedent resolving the exact appellate conflict under Section 531(2)(a) BNSS.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Provide a structured Case Brief and legal assessment on the transitional operation of BNSS Section 531(2)(a) regarding police remand.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE & JURISDICTIONAL THRESHOLD
Whether an investigating agency can lawfully seek police custody remand under Section 187 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) in an investigation arising from an FIR registered prior to 1 July 2024, where the accused has already completed 15 days of judicial custody.

II. GOVERNING RULE & STATUTORY ANATOMY
1. Section 531(2)(a) BNSS provides that if any investigation is pending immediately before 1 July 2024, such investigation "shall be disposed of, continued, held or made... in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973... as if this Sanhita had not come into force."
2. Section 167(2) CrPC strictly limits police custody remand to the first 15 days following the initial production before the Magistrate (CBI v. Anupam J. Kulkarni (1992) 3 SCC 141).
3. Section 187(3) BNSS permits police custody in parts during the first 40 or 60 days, expanding police powers.
4. Controlling Principle: A pending investigation is saved in its entirety under the 1973 Code; the police cannot selectively invoke BNSS provisions to bypass the protective safeguards of the CrPC.

III. APPLICATION TO FACTUAL DISPUTE
1. Gateway Test: The FIR was registered on 10 June 2024. The investigation was legally pending on 30 June 2024. Therefore, Section 531(2)(a) applies unconditionally.
2. Conflict of Codes: The police cannot invoke Section 187 BNSS because the legal fiction of Section 531(2)(a) treats the BNSS as not having come into force for this investigation.
3. Custody Bar: Because more than 15 days have elapsed since initial remand, Section 167(2) CrPC completely bars any grant of police custody.

IV. CONCLUSION & OPERATIVE ADVICE
The application for police remand under Section 187 BNSS is void and without jurisdiction. The Magistrate must reject the remand application and maintain the accused in judicial custody under the provisions of the 1973 CrPC.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Draft comprehensive Written Submissions opposing a police custody remand application under BNSS Section 187 for an offence registered prior to 1 July 2024.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
IN THE COURT OF THE CHIEF METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE, PATIALA HOUSE COURTS, NEW DELHI
CRIMINAL MISC. APPLICATION NO. 782 OF 2024
IN FIR NO. 88 OF 2024 (PS ECONOMIC OFFENCES WING)

IN THE MATTER OF:
STATE (NCT OF DELHI)                      ... PROSECUTION / APPLICANT
VERSUS
PRADEEP SHARMA                           ... ACCUSED / RESPONDENT

WRITTEN SUBMISSIONS ON BEHALF OF THE ACCUSED OPPOSING POLICE REMAND APPLICATION UNDER SECTION 187 BNSS, 2023

MOST RESPECTFULLY SHOWETH:

I. STATEMENT OF MATERIAL FACTS & PROCEDURAL PROVENANCE
1. FIR No. 88 of 2024 was registered at PS EOW on 12 April 2024 under Sections 420, 468, 471, and 120B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
2. The Accused / Respondent was arrested on 14 August 2024 and was remanded to judicial custody after the police did not seek police custody during the initial 15-day period.
3. On 10 September 2024 (27 days post-arrest), the investigating officer filed the instant application under Section 187 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), seeking 7 days of police custody remand, contending that under Section 187(3) BNSS, police custody can be granted in parts throughout the first 40 days of detention.
4. The Accused has filed a preliminary objection on jurisdiction, invoking Section 531(2)(a) BNSS.

II. STATUTORY MANDATE OF SECTION 531(2)(a) BNSS
1. Section 531(2)(a) of the BNSS enacts a mandatory statutory savings clause:
   "if, immediately before the date on which this Sanhita comes into force, there is any appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation pending, then, such appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation shall be disposed of, continued, held or made... in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973... as if this Sanhita had not come into force."
2. The language of Section 531(2)(a) is mandatory, non-discretionary, and clear. The words "shall be disposed of, continued, held or made" leave zero room for judicial or executive deviation.
3. The statutory fiction "as if this Sanhita had not come into force" means that for the purposes of FIR No. 88 of 2024, the BNSS does not exist in the eyes of the law.

III. APPLICABILITY OF SECTION 167(2) CrPC AND THE ABSOLUTE 15-DAY BAR
1. Because the investigation was pending immediately before 1 July 2024, the governing procedural code is strictly the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
2. Under Section 167(2) CrPC, the power of a Magistrate to authorize police custody is restricted strictly to the first 15 days following arrest:
   - Central Bureau of Investigation v. Anupam J. Kulkarni (1992) 3 SCC 141 (Constitution Bench reaffirmation): "There cannot be any police custody after the expiry of the first fifteen days even in a case where some more offences either serious or otherwise committed by him in the same transaction come to light at a later stage."
   - State of Kerala v. Sadanandan (1984) KLT 747.
3. The Accused having completed more than 15 days in judicial custody, the jurisdiction of this Hon'ble Court to grant police custody under the 1973 Code has completely lapsed.

IV. PROSECUTION CANNOT CHERRY-PICK BETWEEN CODES
1. The prosecution cannot selectively treat the investigation as an "old investigation" under the IPC for substantive charges, while treating it as a "new investigation" under the BNSS to exploit coercive police custody powers.
2. In State of Punjab v. Mohar Singh, AIR 1955 SC 84, the Supreme Court ruled that a savings provision preserves both the rights of the citizen and the statutory limitations placed on the State under the repealed law.
3. To permit the prosecution to invoke Section 187 BNSS in a pre-existing FIR would wipe out Section 531(2)(a) and inflict unconstitutional prejudice in violation of Article 21.

V. PRAYER
In the premises aforesaid, the Accused most respectfully prays that this Hon'ble Court may graciously be pleased to:
a. Dismiss the Application for Police Custody Remand filed by the investigating agency as barred by jurisdiction under Section 531(2)(a) BNSS read with Section 167(2) CrPC;
b. Reaffirm that FIR No. 88 of 2024 is governed strictly by the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973; and
c. Pass such further order(s) as this Hon'ble Court may deem fit and proper in the interest of justice.

AND FOR THIS ACT OF JUSTICE, THE ACCUSED SHALL EVER PRAY.

examTips: Always identify the status of the investigation on 30 June 2024 at 23:59:59. If an FIR existed, Section 531(2)(a) saves the 1973 CrPC for the entire life of that case.
Remember the distinction: Article 20(1) protects substantive penal liability (IPC stays for pre-July acts), but does NOT protect procedure. Procedural savings come exclusively from Section 531 BNSS.
Under Section 531(2)(a), police custody cannot be granted in parts under Section 187 BNSS for pre-July 2024 FIRs; the 15-day ceiling under Section 167 CrPC strictly binds the police.
Cite Garikapati Veeraya (1957) and Abdul Khader v. State of Kerala (2024) on the vested right of appeal surviving statutory repeal.
revisionPoints: Governing Provision: Section 531 Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Repeal of CrPC 1973).
Core Savings Gateway: s. 531(2)(a) — pending appeals, applications, trials, inquiries, investigations continue under CrPC as if BNSS had not come into force.
Epoch 1 (Pre-July FIR): IPC + CrPC + IEA (completely saved).
Epoch 2 (Pre-July Crime, Post-July FIR): IPC (Art. 20(1)) + BNSS + BSA.
Leading Authorities: Garikapati Veeraya (1957), Mohar Singh (1955), Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh (1953), Abdul Khader (2024).

learningObjectives: Master the statutory repeal of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 by Section 531(1) BNSS.

enhancement.definition: BNSS s. 531 formally repeals the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 and enacts comprehensive transitional savings. Under Section 531(2)(a), if immediately before 1 July 2024, there is any appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation pending, it shall be disposed of, continued, held or made in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, as in force immediately before such commencement, as if this Sanhita had not come into force.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Procedural continuity, non-disruption of pending judicial administration, and statutory protection of procedural expectations. While procedural amendments are ordinarily retrospective, an express statutory savings clause overrides general retroactivity to ensure orderly legal transition.
statutoryFramework: Sub-section (1): Express repeal of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Act No. 2 of 1974).
Sub-section (2)(a): Foundational savings clause — pending appeals, applications, trials, inquiries, or investigations continue strictly under CrPC 1973.
Sub-section (2)(b): Deeming fiction — actions, notifications, appointments, and orders made under the CrPC continue under corresponding BNSS provisions.
Sub-section (3): Express preservation of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897.
essentialIngredients: The formal repeal of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 with effect from 1 July 2024.
Identification of the procedural stage immediately before 1 July 2024 (pending appeal, application, trial, inquiry, or investigation).
Mandatory application of the saved CrPC 1973 procedure to any pending matter until its final disposal.
Prospective application of BNSS 2023 to all new investigations, applications, and proceedings instituted on or after 1 July 2024.
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Section 531 BNSS is the critical procedural pivot of criminal justice administration post-1 July 2024. When Parliament replaces a procedural code that has governed the nation for fifty years, clear transition rules are essential to prevent jurisdictional confusion.

Under Section 531(1), the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is repealed. However, Section 531(2)(a) contains a comprehensive savings provision. If an investigation was pending on 30 June 2024 (e.g., an FIR registered before 1 July 2024), that investigation must be conducted, completed, and reported under the provisions of the CrPC, 1973. Consequently, police remand in such pending investigations continues to be governed by Section 167 CrPC (where the 15-day police custody can only be granted during the initial 15 days of arrest), rather than Section 187 BNSS (which permits staggering across 40 or 60 days).

Similarly, pending criminal trials and inquiries in which cognizance was taken or charges framed before 1 July 2024 must proceed under the procedural steps of the 1973 Code until final judgment. Appeals arising out of convictions in trials governed by the CrPC are filed and heard in accordance with the saved procedural framework. Conversely, where an FIR is registered on or after 1 July 2024, the entire procedure from investigation to trial is governed exclusively by the BNSS, 2023.

Sub-section (2)(b) ensures institutional continuity: standing notifications, appointments of Special Public Prosecutors, and court territorial distributions made under the CrPC remain valid and are deemed to have been made under the BNSS.
examples: Teaching illustration (Remand in Pre-Commencement FIR): An FIR was registered on 25 June 2024 under the IPC. The accused is arrested on 10 July 2024. The police seek 15 days of police custody on the 25th day after arrest, citing Section 187 BNSS. The Magistrate rejects the application: because the investigation was pending immediately before 1 July 2024, Section 531(2)(a) BNSS mandates that the investigation be conducted under CrPC 1973, where police remand is impermissible beyond the initial 15-day period.

Teaching illustration (Bail Application in Ongoing Trial): An accused has been on trial since 2023 under CrPC procedure. On 10 August 2024, the accused moves a regular bail application before the Sessions Court. Under Section 531(2)(a), the application is governed by Section 439 CrPC 1973 as part of the pending proceeding, though citing Section 483 BNSS does not invalidate the petition.
distinctions: BNSS s. 531 vs BNS s. 358: BNSS s. 531 governs the procedural transition and repeal of the CrPC 1973, whereas BNS s. 358 governs substantive offences and the repeal of the IPC 1860.

BNSS s. 531(2)(a) vs Section 6 General Clauses Act: Section 531(2)(a) explicitly specifies the five procedural stages (appeal, application, trial, inquiry, investigation) that must continue under the old Code, providing greater procedural clarity than general statutory savings.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an appeal against a judgment of conviction pronounced by a Sessions Court on 20 June 2024 must be filed under Section 374 CrPC 1973 or Section 415 BNSS in August 2024.

Rule: Under Section 531(2)(a) BNSS, proceedings, trials, and resultant remedies originating from matters pending immediately before commencement are governed by the saved provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
Application: The trial concluded on 20 June 2024 under the 1973 Code; the right of appeal accrued prior to the commencement of the BNSS.
Conclusion: The appeal is governed by Section 374 of the CrPC, 1973 pursuant to Section 531(2)(a) BNSS.

keyTakeaways: BNSS s. 531 repeals the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
Any investigation, inquiry, trial, application, or appeal pending immediately before 1 July 2024 continues strictly under CrPC 1973.
New proceedings initiated on or after 1 July 2024 are governed exclusively by the BNSS.
Existing appointments, notifications, and rules continue under the deeming fiction of Section 531(2)(b).
